market_context: United States; lactose content of cheese and individual lactose tolerance
title: Cheeses with the least lactose

seo.title: Cheeses with the least lactose
seo.meta_description: Parmesan, Grana Padano, pecorino, Emmental and other aged cheeses can contain only trace lactose. See the numbers and why aging changes them.
seo.search_intent: Identify which cheeses contain the least lactose, approximately how much they provide and why aging lowers lactose.

excerpt: Hard, aged cheeses are usually the lowest in lactose. Analytical reviews place Parmigiano Reggiano, Grana Padano and Pecorino Romano below 0.01 g/100 g, with Emmental, Gruyère and some blue cheeses below 0.1 g/100 g. Actual content varies by process and brand, and lactose intolerance is not the same as milk-protein allergy.
content_html:
Cheese starts with milk, yet some aged cheeses contain hundreds or thousands of times less lactose than milk itself. The reason is what happens during whey drainage, fermentation and ripening. Those processes are why hard aged cheeses dominate a low-lactose list.

The cheeses that repeatedly test lowest

Numbers vary by brand and batch, but analytical reviews show a strong pattern. Properly made and matured examples of these cheeses can reach extremely low levels:

CheeseRepresentative lactoseApproximate amount in 1 oz (28 g)
Parmigiano Reggiano<0.01 g/100 g<0.003 g
Grana Padano<0.01 g/100 g<0.003 g
Pecorino Romano<0.01 g/100 g<0.003 g
Emmental<0.1 g/100 g<0.03 g
Gruyère<0.1 g/100 g<0.03 g
Gorgonzola<0.1 g/100 g<0.03 g
Aged cheddar≈0.1–0.5 g/100 g≈0.03–0.14 g

For context, cow's milk contains roughly 4.5–4.8 g lactose per 100 g. A 1-ounce serving of Parmesan at less than 0.003 g therefore contains well over a thousand times less lactose than 100 g of milk.

Why so much lactose disappears during cheesemaking

Lactose is water soluble. When milk coagulates, much of the lactose leaves with the whey that drains away from the curd. Starter bacteria then consume much of the remaining lactose and convert it to lactic acid.

During extended ripening, that process can reduce residual lactose below laboratory quantification limits. One analysis of protected-origin cheeses found less than 10 mg/kg—under 0.001 g/100 g—in 12-month Parmigiano Reggiano, 9-month Grana Padano, cheddar, Emmental and many other matured cheeses.

Cheddar and Gouda show why “zero” is too absolute

The exact manufacturing process matters as much as the cheese name. One clinical review uses around 0.5 g/100 g for cheddar, while standardized mature cheddars in analytical studies have tested below 0.015 g/100 g. Published Gouda samples range from less than 0.02 g/100 g to roughly 0.14 g/100 g.

“Aged cheese” is therefore a useful clue, not a guaranteed laboratory value. Anyone who needs very precise lactose control should rely on manufacturer information or a specifically lactose-free product rather than assuming a number from the cheese name alone.

Fresh cheeses generally contain much more

At the other end are cheeses that retain more whey and undergo little or no aging. Clinical reviews report roughly 3.2 g lactose/100 g for cottage cheese, about 1.4 g/100 g for feta, and values around 1.5–3.3 g/100 g for mozzarella, depending on the product and analysis.

That does not mean everyone with lactose intolerance must avoid them. Symptom thresholds vary substantially between people and also depend on serving size and whether the food is eaten with a meal.

Lactose intolerance is not milk allergy

Lactose intolerance is difficulty digesting the sugar lactose. Milk allergy is an immune reaction to milk proteins. A cheese with almost no lactose still contains milk proteins and is not made safe for someone with a milk allergy simply by aging.

NIDDK also notes that many people with lactose intolerance can tolerate some lactose. Research suggests many can consume around 12 g in one sitting with no symptoms or only mild symptoms. An ounce of a hard cheese containing less than 0.1 g/100 g supplies under 0.03 g, a very different dose.

The useful takeaway

If minimizing lactose is the goal, start with hard, well-aged cheeses: Parmigiano Reggiano, Grana Padano, Pecorino Romano, Emmental and Gruyère are consistently low examples. Treat the figures as ranges for real products, not as an immutable property of every cheese with the same name.

faq.question: Which cheese has the least lactose?
faq.answer: Parmigiano Reggiano, Grana Padano and Pecorino Romano repeatedly test below 0.01 g lactose/100 g in analytical reviews, although exact products can vary.

faq.question: Does aged cheese contain zero lactose?
faq.answer: Many aged cheeses contain only trace amounts, but it is not accurate to assume every aged cheese is literally zero. Whey drainage, cultures and aging time all affect the final value.

faq.question: How much lactose is in cheddar?
faq.answer: Published values vary. Clinical reviews use about 0.5 g/100 g as a representative figure, while some standardized mature cheddars test below 0.015 g/100 g.

faq.question: Is lactose-free cheese safe for a milk allergy?
faq.answer: No. Removing lactose does not remove the milk proteins that trigger a milk allergy.
